articles.title_orig: White Sox 7, Astros 3: A postseason series victory
articles.title_zh: White Sox 7, Astros 3: A postseason series victory
articles.content_orig:
7:46 PM CDT on September 30, 2026
Erick Fedde celebrates the final out.
In the 57 years Major League Baseball has made it possible to win a postseason series without winning the World Series, the White Sox had only one one in one season -- 2005, when they won the whole thing.
That count is up to two, and this series ended the same as the last one, with the White Sox sealing a sweep in Houston's ballpark.
The White Sox knocked Hunter Brown out of the first inning with a four-run blitz, and when three Astros solo shots narrowed the margin to one, Chase Meidroth regained the ground in the sixth inning with a resounding three-run blast off Bryan Abreu. The White Sox bullpen, which wobbled out of the gate, ended up throwing five scoreless innings to exit Houston as victors.
Meidroth's clout will probably stand as the defining image of this series, especially since the White Sox barely escaped the previous inning with the lead intact.
Huascar Brazobán entered in relief of Sean Burke with a 4-3 lead in the fifth inning and promptly plunked Cam Smith. He struck out Nick Allen to gain some footing, but a single to Jeremy Peña brought Yordan Alvarez to the plate without a base open.
Will Venable countered with Anthony Kay, who fell behind 3-0 ... and still got him out, spotting an outside-corner fastball that Alvarez sliced to Sam Antonacci in left for the second out. Kay then fell behind Isaac Paredes and walked him on four pitches to load the bases. Jose Altuve, who hit one of the three homers off Burke earlier in the game, made Kay throw a fastball strike, but got a well-located changeup on the second pitch, and flied out to right to strand three.
That provided temporary relief, but the White Sox now had to solve their problems on offense, which ground to a halt once Brown left the game. Antonacci grounded out with the bases loaded to start a streak of 13 consecutive batters retired by AJ Blubaugh and Peter Lambert, the prospective Game 3 starter who ended up taking over in the third.
The Sox finally snapped the streak when Andrew Benintendi took a full-count fastball low for a leadoff walk in the top of the sixth. Luisangel Acuña pinch-ran for him and stole second, although the effects were negated when Tristan Peters walked on four pitches. That's when Joe Espada went to the bullpen for his top right-handed reliever, Bryan Abreu, to face Chase Meidroth.
Initially, the White Sox were going to concede the matchup as Meidroth showed bunt on Abreu's first pitch. But Acuña and Peters took off on Abreu's first pitch, which nobody on the Astros anticipated for the kind of incredibly easy double steal the White Sox have been used to allowing. That allowed Meidroth to swing away, and did he ever.
First, he watched two more pitches out of the zone to make it a 3-0 count. He took all the way on a fastball strike, and when Abreu went to the slider on 3-1, Abreu left it over the inner half, and Meidroth uncoiled on it, sending it off the left field wall above the yellow line for a three-run blast that set the White Sox dugout ablaze and allowed White Sox fans to breathe a huge sigh of relief.
Thanks to Jordan Hicks and Erick Fedde, blood pressures remained settled the rest of the evening. Hicks retired all six batters he faced to go 10-for-10 over the two games, and Fedde did the same as the unlikely final pitcher.
The sweep indicated how thoroughly the White Sox outplayed the Astros. Brown came into this game 6-0 in six starts against Chicago, but thanks to a series of line drives and miscues, he departed with only two outs in the first and trailing 4-0.
Sam Antonacci started the game by exploiting a compromised Astros defense. Houston started Alvarez in left field due to Paredes' knee issue, and Antonacci lined a drive over his outstretched glove in left center for a leadoff double. Kyle Teel then shot a single past a diving Altuve, and the White Sox had a 1-0 lead in just five pitches.
Miguel Vargas followed with a bouncer to third, but Nick Allen's attempt to smother the hop deflected off him and into foul territory for an E-5. Brown rebounded to strike out Munetaka Murakami, but Andrew Benintendi picked him up with a broken-bat single to center that scored Teel, and then Vargas when an ill-advised throw from center escaped catcher Yainer Diaz. Tristan Peters then got on top of a high fastball for a single to right center that scored Benintendi to make it 4-0.
Brown gave up a single to Meidroth and struck out Braden Montgomery to bring up ninth-hitting Colson Montgomery, but a walk turned over the lineup and ended his night. The move worked, as Blubaugh got Antonacci to ground out to avoid an even bigger disaster.
From there, the Astros offense chipped away. Jeremy Peña greeted Burke with a homer to get Houston on the board, Cam Smith hit a bomb in the second, and Altuve made it three over four innings by dropping one in the Crawford Boxes to make it a 4-3 game.
That said, the adage that solo shots won't kill you proved correct enough. Burke allowed only one other hit and zero walks while striking out eight, so while the Astros killed his mistakes, there were no multiplying factors. He didn't quite get the game to the halfway point, but while the Sox used four relievers, everybody will get the next two full days off.

*The Sox once again found production without their biggest bats, as Vargas and Murakami went 0-for-10 with five strikeouts in the middle of the order.
*The Sox were 4-for-9 with runners in scoring position, while the Astros were 0-for-2. They won both the denominator and the numerator.
*The Sox also played errorless ball, with Vargas making up for his Game 1 error by stabbing an Alvarez hot shot as the only defender on the left side.
*Alvarez finished the series 1-for-8 with two strikeouts.

articles.content_orig:
Federal prosecutors have unsealed indictments against 10 people who falsely claimed they were citizens when voting or registering to vote in Minnesota.
According to the U.S. Department of Justice, the defendants include foreign nationals from Bosnia and Herzegovina, Brazil, Canada, Germany, Ghana, Liberia, Lithuania, and South Africa:
Charges against the defendants include falsely claiming citizenship in order to vote and voting by an alien, most recently in the August 2026 primary election.
The indictments do not include any details on where the defendants registered to vote or how they managed to cast a ballot.
At least one of the defendants, Weihmann, is already charged in state court.
RELATED: DOJ files misconduct complaint against Minnesota judges over comments about Metro Surge
During a news conference in Washington alongside U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, U.S. Attorney for Minnesota Daniel Rosen said the alleged crimes arise from “a general tolerance for fraud” in Minnesota.
According to the Minnesota Secretary of State’s Office, 3,272,414 votes were cast in the 2024 general election. Minnesota Judicial Branch records show 57 charges of ineligible voters knowingly voting filed statewide from 2021-25, 14 of which resulted in convictions.
Felony charges filed against Weihmann last year in Isanti County reveal she is a green card holder who resides in Cambridge, Minnesota, and has been in the country since 2015.
According to a criminal complaint, Weihmann cast ballots in 2022 and 2024 and filled out paperwork to inactivate her voter record when an election official informed her she was ineligible to vote. Isanti County election administrators referred the case to the sheriff’s office for investigation.
Weihmann faces two charges of knowingly voting as an ineligible voter in Isanti County District Court. A plea hearing is scheduled for Oct. 7.

articles.title_orig: Sean Combs’ release date is pushed up, as new report details pampered prison lifestyle
articles.title_zh: Sean Combs’ release date is pushed up, as new report details pampered prison lifestyle
articles.content_orig:
Inside the walls of Fort Dix federal prison in New Jersey, no one is living quite like inmate #37452-054.
There are men who cook for him and men who clean for him. There are men who make his bed and men who do his laundry. There is even a man who gives him Chinese-style massages.
This is how Sean “Diddy” Combs has been living in prison, according to four men who have spent time in the same unit as the disgraced hip-hop mogul. They were granted anonymity to speak freely about life inside the prison.
“This is not some normal s--- you see in jail. This is some rich s---,” said one of the men. “It looks crazy, but again, it’s Diddy.”
This story is also drawn in part from photos and videos taken inside the prison and reviewed by NBC News. They include footage of Combs appearing to use a contraband phone.
Diddy appears to use cellphone in prison
Combs, 56, is serving a 50-month sentence for prostitution-related offenses. But he is still living a privileged life, the sources said, and it’s not just because of the inmates willing to perform even the most basic tasks for him for the right price.
Multiple sources said he uses contraband cellphones to scroll Instagram and scan nude and sexually explicit photos that an old girlfriend sends him. He’s been able to buy from other inmates an antidepressant drug sought out for its mood-boosting effects — Remeron, or “rem-roms” as they are known in prison. On weekend nights, he’d often tap into a secret stash of premium liquor, which would be smuggled in by guards and shared with a tight group of fellow inmates.
“Hell yeah, I drank with him,” said one of the men, who recounted drinking Hennessy with Combs.
A spokesperson for Combs downplayed the details of his prison life.
“The continued scrutiny of every mundane detail of Sean Combs’s life in prison has reached the point where the media characterizes ordinary prison life as news,” the spokesperson said. “The only real news is that Sean continues to serve his sentence while awaiting the court’s decision on his appeal.”
A Bureau of Prisons spokesperson said the agency does not comment on a particular inmate’s conditions due to “privacy, safety and security reasons.”
“Like all correctional agencies, contraband, particularly cell phones, narcotics, and weapons, remains a constant challenge, and we continue to tackle the problem of contraband being introduced into our facilities,” the spokesperson added in a statement.
Combs’ exalted existence behind bars doesn’t come cheap.
He has spent thousands of dollars a month to bring his lifestyle to the low-security prison, sources said, with the money flowing from people outside prison to the commissary accounts of those inmates performing services for him.
Those paid by Combs include a man who would clean the toilet and shower areas before he’d use them, and men who would secretly cook him special meals — curry chicken, pizza, empanadas — using a makeshift heating element submerged in water, sources said.
“After a while, I got tired of cooking,” said one man who described preparing meals for Combs and other inmates. “He started going to the Jamaicans.”
There are also inmates who hold on to Combs’ phone and fan mail for him.
“It’s so much that he gets,” one of the sources said. “He doesn’t have room for it.”
Like many other state and federal prisons across the U.S., Fort Dix has grappled with a contraband problem . Just last week, five people, including a current and former corrections officer, were charged with running a scheme to smuggle illicit items into the South Jersey prison. The contraband included knives, marijuana and cellphones, federal prosecutors said.
Since 2020, authorities have also charged multiple people for allegedly using drones to drop illicit goods into the Fort Dix prison yard or atop a roof . The suspects have included inmates and outside accomplices who had previously served time at the facility. In one case, Fort Dix staff intercepted a 46-pound laundry bag filled with contraband.
Combs isn’t the first famous person to receive special treatment behind bars. Harvey Weinstein, for one, was held in a private room at the Rikers Island jail in New York, with access to his own phone, bathroom and television, according to The City Reporter .
The massive Fort Dix prison, 60 miles southwest of New York City, houses about 4,000 inmates.
Combs arrived there in October following his conviction on two counts of transporting people across state lines for sexual encounters.
The trial featured lurid testimony about highly choreographed sexual encounters Combs organized called “freak offs.” They involved male sex workers, elaborate costumes, drugs and former girlfriends — including the singer Cassie — who filed a lawsuit against Combs alleging years of physical and sexual abuse. (The case was settled, with Combs denying any wrongdoing.)
His trial ended in a split verdict, with a New York jury finding him not guilty on sex trafficking and racketeering charges that could have put him in prison for life.
Following his sentencing, Combs’ lawyers pushed for him to be sent to Fort Dix in part because it offers a drug treatment program. Completing the monthslong program often leads to a reduction of an inmate’s prison term, making it highly coveted.
Combs entered the program upon his arrival at Fort Dix. Sources said it took little time for him to acquire a phone, alcohol and a growing number of inmates on his payroll.
“Pretty much the day he arrived, the party started,” one of the sources said.
Many Fort Dix inmates consume alcohol and Remeron, sources said. The medication is prescribed to inmates suffering from depression and anxiety. But it’s also bought and sold on the prison’s robust black market, the sources said.
“You can pretty much get anything except a key to the front door and a female,” one of the sources said.
Among the items Combs has gotten his hands on, two sources said, is a “jailbroken” tablet that he has used to watch movies and documentaries — including “Sean Combs: The Reckoning,” the Netflix docuseries produced by his longtime nemesis 50 Cent.
His presence at the prison has also led to some surreal moments, the sources said. In his first few days, he would walk around in only a towel or boxer shorts after a shower, prompting inmates to warn him that he could be targeted for sex.
“That’s not normal,” one of the sources said.
Over the summer Combs was placed in solitary confinement following a fight with another inmate, NBC News reported in July . He was later kicked out of the drug treatment program, sources said.
But after he was moved out of solitary, the sources said, he went right back to living the life great wealth can buy you in prison, with a team of inmates catering to him.
“He’s a billionaire. People are in awe of him,” said one of the sources. “Money is power, especially behind bars.”
Rich Schapiro is a reporter with the NBC News national security unit.

articles.title_orig: BBC paying to air shows like Suits and Schitt's Creek is illogical, MPs say
articles.title_zh: BBC paying to air shows like Suits and Schitt's Creek is illogical, MPs say
articles.content_orig:
The BBC should not pay "over the odds" for the rights to overseas hits such as Suits and Schitt's Creek, an influential group of MPs has said.
It is one of several issues raised in a wide-ranging report about the BBC's funding and future, published by the House of Commons' cross-party culture and media committee.
Although the BBC produces a lot of its own programmes, the corporation buys some international shows for its TV channels and iPlayer streaming platform.
The MPs' report said the BBC could "spend more wisely when competing for programming". Overall, the BBC brings "immeasurable benefits" to society but needs reform of the TV licence fee to avoid a fate of "managed decline", they said.
Committee chair Dame Caroline Dinenage said the report comes at "a pivotal moment for the BBC", which is grappling with changing media habits, declining income and negotiations with the government over how it is paid for.
Dame Caroline said the government "must ensure the BBC has a universal and sustainable source of funding".
But, she added, the BBC "can play its part by sweating its assets and boxing clever for the licence payer by ending illogical practices such as outbidding commercial rivals for overseas hits such as Suits, Schitt's Creek and Scooby Doo".
The rights to air all three programmes were bought by the BBC after contracts with other networks or streaming services expired.
"At a time of constrained resources, the BBC should not be paying over the odds for overseas content, particularly when it's a bidding war against commercial UK broadcasters," the committee said.
The MPs added that they "did not believe that this provides value for money for the licence fee payer".
The BBC said it spends less than 5% of its content budget on acquiring shows, less than other broadcasters, and they are a cost-effective way of delivering high-quality content to audiences who go on to discover homegrown programming.
The committee's report has been published as the government considers its options for the next BBC Royal Charter, which will set out how the broadcaster will be governed, regulated and funded from 2028 onwards.
Dame Caroline said: "For all its faults, the BBC drives our creative economy, supports our democracy through media sovereignty, and delivers world-class entertainment and moments that bring us together.
"Like a much-loved family member, we may criticise and grumble about the BBC but we would miss it enormously if it were no longer here for us."
The committee said there were "considerable challenges" for the BBC and warned that the current TV licence fee is "outdated and no longer fit for purpose".
Currently, about 94% of individuals use the BBC each month but only 80% of households pay for a TV licence, the MPs noted.
"The licence fee should be reformed so it is no longer linked to the consumption of live TV or to a particular device, such as a television set," the committee said.
"This should be an easier sell to licence fee payers if expanding the base is paired with a drop in the individual cost."
The BBC's director-general Matt Brittin has previously described the current licence fee model as "a busted flush" and "yesterday's model", and has said the price could be cut if more people pay under an overhauled system.
The committee also suggested the BBC should:
The committee suggested the government should:
The committee supported opening up BBC iPlayer to shows from other public service broadcasters such as Channel 4.
Earlier this week, Channel 4 chief executive Priya Dogra said she was open to her network's content being hosted on iPlayer.
The report also called for the end of political appointments to the BBC board, to improve governance and remain trusted by the public.
And the committee recommended that the BBC is given new public purposes relating to innovation and technology and combating misinformation and disinformation.
The BBC welcomed the report, which it said made "some important and interesting recommendations on the future of the BBC".
A BBC spokesperson said: "We have consistently argued that the current funding model is outdated and needs reform, so we welcome the Committee's support for maintaining universal funding while overhauling the licence fee.
"We are also pleased to see their recognition of the vital work of the World Service, with a clear recommendation that responsibility for funding should return fully to Government.
"At a time of huge disruption in the media, the BBC's trust, reach and creative strength remain unparalleled. But we also recognise the need to evolve and move faster towards the future."
The government's Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS) said it "agrees entirely with the Committee's conclusion that it is in the country's best interests for the next Charter to support an ambitious and innovative BBC, and that the corporation cannot be left to a future of managed decline".
A DCMS spokesperson added: "We will review and consider the committee's recommendations in detail, alongside the views of the public and other stakeholders, to inform decisions for the next Royal Charter."

Windows 11 26H2 is here earlier than expected, but before you run off and install it, you might want to take a second. Microsoft has issued a warning that the update contains a few known issues.
According to the Windows Release Health notes :
To be clear, these issues aren’t caused by Windows 11 26H2. In fact, Windows 11 versions 25H2 and 24H2 also show those same issues on their respective Windows Release Health pages. However, it’s possible for your PC to not be experiencing these issues now but start experiencing them once you upgrade to Windows 11 26H2. Meanwhile, if you’re already experiencing them, you’ll likely keep experiencing them post-update.
While Microsoft has marked these issues as “mitigated,” the reality is that they still persist and Microsoft is still investigating solutions.
If you haven’t yet noticed the issues above and absolutely don’t want them to happen on your PC, you should wait until Microsoft reports that these issues have been fixed before installing Windows 11 26H2. (That’s our recommendation, not Microsoft’s.) It’s unclear how long it’ll be before those fixes are released—Microsoft hasn’t provided details.

articles.content_orig:
Anthropic says its AI models could pose a “catastrophic or existential risk to humanity” and can “resist shutdown,” according to an initial public offering prospectus obtained by Reuters.
Anthropic is pursuing an IPO some time in the next year that many expect to value the five-year-old company at approximately $2 trillion. The company’s Wall Street debut will follow a June public offering by SpaceX, which owed much of its $2 trillion opening day valuation to its own AI efforts. OpenAI , the other leading American AI company, has announced plans for its own public offering.
The Anthropic IPO could raise tens of billions of dollars for the cash-hungry company. But the company behind Claude also warned in the prospectus that its AI models can have “self-preserving behaviors” and have attempted to “conceal or manipulate information” and engaged in behavior “resembling blackmail” according to the report.
Why AI companies are choosing to go public
The run of AI public offerings not only gives individual and institutional investors a chance to cash in on the AI boom, but also provides more transparency about their businesses. Yet the IPOs come amid growing concerns about AI’s advancement and capabilities.
An AI agent from OpenAI, Anthropic’s chief rival, broke into an Australian healthcare database, the country’s prime minister revealed last week. OpenAI also disclosed Friday that its agents probed three US government websites without authorization, but in that case did not obtain non-public data.
In a prospectus, companies typically offer investors lists of risks they face, such as lawsuits and competitive pressures, when laying out the case for investing in the company. But the hazards are never this stark. Anthropic dedicated 80 pages to its risk factors in the leaked prospectus, significantly more than the 48 pages it spent detailing its business, according to Reuters.
Anthropic did not respond to a request for comment from CNN.
The prospectus is likely to feed growing concerns about the risks posed to humanity by AI. Earlier this month, former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon received widespread attention when he left the company and posted on X that “the people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.”
Anthropic is one of the leading companies in AI development, and its CEO Dario Amodei responded to Coxon’s post with a 3,800 word essay calling for a slowdown and guardrails on the development of AI. He also told CNN’s Anderson Cooper that he agreed with Coxon more than he disagreed. Amodei wrote in his essay that the risks are serious, even if the benefits could change humanity for the better.
Some in the industry, however, including the CEO of Hugging Face, which was breached by OpenAI’s AI models when they acted without authorization during a test, believe the fears are overblown.
President Donald Trump is set to meet with executives from the industry Tuesday, including Amodei, in a summit aimed at coming to a consensus in the industry. Trump has repeatedly resisted calls to regulate AI and has dismissed concerns as a “hoax.”
AI stocks slide after top industry CEOs call for slowdown of technology’s development
AI giants need to raise a great amount of money to fund their costly development plans, and the massive amount of AI spending among big tech companies on computing infrastructure and talent has sent jitters through Wall Street.
The leaked Anthropic IPO filing sheds light on its financials, revealing that the company lost $42 billion in 2025, according to Reuters. The company plans to spend $518 billion on cloud computing and infrastructure obligations in coming year, and said that nearly a quarter of its revenue last year came from two customers.
Anthropic was last valued at $965 billion in May.

articles.title_orig: Everything Chad Lowe has said about fatherhood before daughter Fiona’s devastating death
articles.title_zh: Everything Chad Lowe has said about fatherhood before daughter Fiona’s devastating death
articles.content_orig:
Chad Lowe often gushed about being a father to his three daughters before his middle child, Fiona, died in September 2026 at age 13.
During a December 2025 interview on the “Still Here Hollywood” podcast , the former “Life Goes On” actor shared what it was like being a “girl dad.”
“It’s so interesting because always wanting to have my own experiences and not live in the shadow or follow in the footsteps of somebody, I get the experience of being a girl dad, which is such a privilege,” he said at the time.
“And I feel bad for anyone who’s a parent … I feel like having daughters is such an incredible privilege because it takes what I have known intellectually about women and all the equality and the glass ceiling that’s there, and how it’s a misogynistic world in many ways,” Lowe, who shares daughters Mabel, 17, Fiona and Nixie, 10, with wife Kim Painter, shared.
“And now it’s taken what I’ve known, and it’s put it in my heart because I now have three daughters. So, I look at the world from, really, their perspective.”
Last February, weeks after devastating Los Angeles-area fires destroyed their house, Lowe shared an Instagram post of his family returning to what once was their home.
“Almost a month after we evacuated our girls finally got to go back to see what’s left of their home,” he captioned the post.
The “Pretty Little Liars” alum, 58, said the way his wife and daughters handled losing their home of more than a decade was “nothing short of remarkable.”
“I am in awe of their spirit and resilience. Helping them navigate these tough times is my sole purpose. Being their dad is my life’s greatest joy and privilege ⭐️⭐️⭐️,” he added.
Last November, Lowe took to Instagram to celebrate Fiona entering her teenage years.
Start your day with Page Six Daily.
“Celebrating Fiona officially becoming a teen today!! Keep dancing through life FiBear! Love you soooo much!!”
During a 2024 family ski trip to Mammoth Mountain in California, Lowe said he didn’t “take one moment of it for granted.” He added the hashtags “blessed” and “girl dad.”
As Page Six previously reported, Lowe’s daughter Fiona passed away. She was weeks shy of her 14th birthday.
“We are deeply heartbroken by the loss of our beloved Fiona. She was a loving young girl who was smart, creative and loved to dance,” her family shared in a statement to Page Six on Tuesday.
“She was adored by her sisters and she was deeply loved by her parents. In fact, she was the light of our lives. Her passing is devastating for our entire family and we ask for prayers and privacy at this time,” they added.
“If you or someone you know is struggling with mental health, please reach out to the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline by calling or texting 988.”
It’s unclear how the teen died and her family has not disclosed any other information.
Chad — who is the younger brother of actor Rob Lowe — and Painter have been married since August 2010.
They welcomed Mabel in May 2009, followed by Fiona and Nixie in November 2012 and March 2016, respectively.
If you or someone you know is affected by any of the issues raised in this story, call the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 800-273-TALK (8255) or text Crisis Text Line at 741741.
If you are struggling with suicidal thoughts, you can dial the 24/7 National Suicide Prevention Hotline at 988 or go to SuicidePreventionLifeline.org .

articles.title_orig: Tyson Fury: Anthony Joshua the landlord? 'I'm not paying!'
articles.title_zh: Tyson Fury: Anthony Joshua the landlord? 'I'm not paying!'
articles.content_orig:
(This story first appeared on USA Today Sports . )
Jake Paul took a verbal shot Wednesday, Sept. 30 during the press conference to promote the heavyweight fight between Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury.
It came from Turki Alalshikh, the Saudi government official who has led that country's efforts to promote big fights. Such as Fury vs. Joshua.
"Big thanks to the champion…'' Alalshikh said, referring to Joshua during the press event in London. "AJ helped boxing and saved boxing with Netflix, kicking out YouTuber from the boxing.''
Of course that YouTuber is Paul.
Joshua broke Paul's jaw in two places with a knockout blow during their fight on Dec. 19 . The punch came in the sixth round, and Paul was knocked down a total of four times during the fight in Miami.
Paul has not boxed since that brutal knockout.
After the bout, he went to the hospital, where he had surgery.
Paul, 27, had a second surgery and has yet to resume training, although he has said he's negotiating with potential opponents for his next fight .
Paul is 12-2 with seven knockouts, and while sidelined from boxing, has been visible with entrepreneurial projects and as co-founder of Most Valuable Promotions.
